lessons.title: عفوا (ʿafwan) — "you're welcome," from a root meaning "to erase"
lessons.gloss: "you're welcome" (also "excuse me/pardon/sorry," depending on context) — root ʿ-f-w, "to erase, to pardon"; grammatically the same construction as shukran itself

segments.text: Your very first Arabic lesson already used this word once, in passing, as the reply to shukran. Here it gets its own full treatment — starting with a root that literally means "to erase."

عفوا (ʿafwan), root ʿ-f-w (ع-ف-و): the root's core sense is "to erase, obliterate, remove" — and "to pardon, forgive" grows directly out of that, since forgiving something is, metaphorically, erasing it. The same root gives العفو (al-ʿAfuww, "the Supreme Pardoner"), one of the 99 names of Allah in Islamic tradition.

blocks.title: You'll want to know — Be honest: ʿafwan does more than one job

segments.text: ʿAfwan answers shukran as "you're welcome" — but depending on tone and context, the exact same word also does duty as "excuse me," "pardon," or "sorry." One root, one word, several closely related jobs — all growing from that same "erase/pardon" sense.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the same ending as shukran itself

segments.text: Look closely at the spelling: عفوا ends in the same tanwīn fatḥ ("-an") you already met in شكرا (shukran) — the indefinite accusative ending. Neither word is a full sentence with its own verb; both are fixed, idiomatic accusative forms functioning as a complete conversational turn on their own. The grammar you learned once, for shukran, already explains ʿafwan too.

segments.instruction: the root ʿ-f-w — "to erase" becomes "to pardon"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the root ʿ-f-w — "to erase" → "to pardon"]

segments.instruction: the shared ending — shukran and ʿafwan both end in the same tanwīn fatḥ, "-an"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the shared ending — shukran and ʿafwan both end in the same tanwīn fatḥ, "-an"]

segments.text: What does the root ʿ-f-w literally mean, before it comes to mean "pardon"? ("To erase, obliterate.") Besides "you're welcome," what other jobs can ʿafwan do? ("Excuse me," "pardon," "sorry" — context-dependent.) What grammatical ending does ʿafwan share with shukran? (The tanwīn fatḥ, "-an" — both are fixed indefinite- accusative forms, not full sentences.)

lessons.title: Please, sorry, thank you
lessons.gloss: the courtesy kit retrieved whole — yes, please, sorry and thank you, the two letters that write the last of them, and the fact that three of the four bend to the person you are speaking to

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
waitUntilStopped: Script: the two letters inside شكرا
Writing: what changes when letters join
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script: the two letters inside شكرا and Writing: what changes when letters join until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Say yes, please, sorry and thank you in Arabic, in that order, before reading on. Four short words, each taught once, none asked for since.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: three of the four bend

utterances: word: please. to a man: من فضلك min faḍlak. to a woman: من فضلك min faḍlik.
word: sorry. to a man: آسف āsif. to a woman: آسفة āsifa.
word: yes. to a man: نعم naʿam. to a woman: نعم naʿam.

segments.text: Naʿam is the clear standard yes, safe anywhere, and it has spoken neighbours you will also hear. Min faḍlik is the only one of the three whose bend is invisible: the written form does not change at all, because only the unwritten short vowel moves.

آسف is stranger than English sorry, because it is not a fixed word — it is a gendered adjective, from the verb asifa, to grieve or regret. So a woman apologising says a different word from a man. For a quick, ungendered excuse me, Arabic reaches for معذرة maʿdhira instead.

blocks.title: Script: the two letters inside شكرا

segments.text: ش shīn is not a new shape at all: it is س sīn with three dots on top — the same trick the boat-bowl plays, where ب takes one dot below, ت two above and ث three above. The dots do the work; the skeleton is shared.
The other new letter in the word is ك kāf.

blocks.title: Writing: what changes when letters join

segments.instruction: سلام right to left — sīn, lām, alif, mīm
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: **سلام** right to left — *sīn · lām · alif · mīm*]

segments.instruction: شكرا — shīn with its three dots, then kāf, rāʾ, alif
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: **شكرا** — *shīn* with its three dots, then *kāf*, *rāʾ*, *alif*]

segments.text: What changes when a letter joins is the connector at each edge. What stays is the skeleton — which is why a letter you learned standing alone is still readable buried in the middle of a word.

The reply to thanks is عفوا ʿafwan — it is nothing, you are pardoned — from a root meaning to forgive or waive. English answers gratitude by accepting it. Arabic answers by waving it away: you thank, and they erase the debt.

Give the two forms of sorry and what makes them differ. (آسف and آسفة — a gendered adjective.) Give the reply to شكرا and its literal force. (عفوا — it is nothing, you are pardoned.) Say what ش is made of. (س plus three dots.) And say which courtesy word bends without the spelling changing. (من فضلك.)
